title: The history of tapestry in Europe

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Tapestries are a wonderful record of our history. They are created by weaving different coloured threads together to produce beautiful and detailed images. The art of tapestry weaving goes back thousands of years and appears in diverse cultures. Both the ancient Egyptians and the Incas buried their dead in tapestry woven clothing. Important civic buildings of the Greek Empire, including the Parthenon, had walls covered with them.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Tapestries became symbols of elevated status amongst the European aristocracy in the medieval period (5th-15th century). They also had much practical use: they provided insulation when placed on cold and damp castle walls, they were used to cover openings, and they also provided privacy around beds for aristocrats. Kings took them on their royal travels from castle to castle for reasons of comfort and to show how rich and powerful they were.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: It has been estimated that 15,000 people were employed in medieval tapestry weaving. Many of them were people who moved around frequently and passed their skills down through the family – from father to son. At this time, it would take a skilled father and son team two months to weave just 900 square centimetres of tapestry. The tapestries of the time had a range of fewer than twenty colours and medieval weavers extracted the dyes for the threads used in their tapestries from plants and insects. For example, red came from poppies or pomegranates, and woad (a plant from the cabbage family) produced blue.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: In medieval Europe, most people were illiterate so, at this time, the Church recognised the usefulness of tapestries – religious stories could be illustrated on them and people could see these tapestries and learn the stories without having to read the Bible. Only a few of this kind of tapestry have survived until the present day. The oldest existing set of tapestries of this kind is the Apocalypse of St John. It tells a story in ninety colourful scenes, each of which has either a red or blue background. It consists of six tapestries, each 5.5 metres high, totalling 144 metres in length, which were woven in Paris between 1375 and 1379.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The most popular medieval images were legends, myths, allegories – the ever-popular unicorn represented purity – and contemporary scenes of peasants working or nobles hunting. Battle scenes were commissioned by victorious kings and queens. The Holy Roman Emperor Charles V was even accompanied into battle by his court painter, who made sketches at the site for later weaving. Hunting scenes led to tapestries of lush landscapes. Medieval weavers worked from basic rough sketches, which they freely adapted with imagination and sometimes humour. However, these sketches had become far more detailed by the time of the Renaissance (15th18th century) and were full-sized cartoons, which were rigidly copied by the weavers.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: In Renaissance France, during the lavish reign of King Louis XIV, a remarkable new facility was established at Les Gobelins. This was a large building in Paris where over 800 artisans produced tapestries for the King's court on a scale never before seen. Other European countries followed suit, opening similar establishments on behalf of their rulers. They employed Flemish weavers, who by now had to study and carry out supervised work to complete a twelve-year apprenticeship. When Louis XIV died, the list of his belongings included 2,155 Gobelins tapestries. Similarly, King Henry VIII's collection totalled over 2,000 spread among his seventeen royal residences.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The history of tapestries underwent major changes during the French Revolution and shortly afterwards. The social developments of the time affected the tapestry market so negatively that the government ordered 190 of them to be burnt because they considered the gold and silver threads in the tapestries to have greater value than the tapestries as a whole. A positive development of this period, however, was the invention in 1804 of a machine called the Jacquard mechanical loom, on which tapestries could be made. It enabled tapestries to become accessible to a wider market and it still forms the basis of the tapestry making techniques used today.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Today few tapestries are hand-woven. Most are reproductions of originals in museums. Modern threads and techniques allow us to enjoy wonderful copies of works of art at affordable prices. Nonetheless, much work is still required to produce them, especially during the design stage. Fortunately, some use can be made of computers to reduce the time involved in weaving a tapestry but much skill and experience is still required. The weavers match the thread colours from a selection of about 1,000 shades. Cotton, often combined with viscose, is used for the fine detail of smaller tapestries, while wool can be introduced to add greater fullness and richness to large pieces.
